prompt.context: Mercado Reforma is a large B2B grocery supplier in Latin America that wants to expand into the B2C space. Note: Reforma has no history or experience in the B2C space but has extensive distribution networks and expects refining their operations and scaling will not be insurmountable challenges. Reforma currently operates in Mexico, Chile, and Colombia. While the company operates across the entirety of these countries, the majority of their distribution capabilities are concentrated in Mexico City, Santiago, and Bogota. Their goal is to enter the market in an innovative way. Reforma believes there is whitespace in the food services industry for an unmet customer need, but is currently unsure what that looks like in practice. A primary focus of the engagement should be to ensure the proposed market entry strategy embodies the voice of the customer, addressing customer needs and frustrations.
prompt.question: You are the project leader. Ideate ways to investigate the opportunity and bring the concept to life. Walk me through how you would approach the project.

clarifying_info.q: Does Reforma have any experience in the B2C space?
clarifying_info.a: No history or experience in B2C, but they have extensive distribution networks and expect scaling will not be an insurmountable challenge.
Mexico, Chile, and Colombia. Distribution capabilities are concentrated in Mexico City, Santiago, and Bogota.

clarifying_info.q: What is Reforma's goal for market entry?
clarifying_info.a: They want to enter in an innovative way. They believe there is whitespace for an unmet customer need in food services but are unsure what that looks like in practice.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a specific customer segment to focus on?
clarifying_info.a: A primary focus is to ensure the proposed strategy embodies the voice of the customer — addressing customer needs and frustrations.

exhibits.title: Customer Persona: Millennials on the Move
exhibits.shows: A customer persona card for millennial urban professionals in Latin American megacities (CDMX residents pictured). Lists their needs and frustrations related to food access and time constraints.

needs: Accessible food options when on the go out in the city
Food options that better cater to their dietary preferences
Ability to pick-up cooked food or bundled ingredients when pressed for time
Options that allow for a quick and efficient shopping or pick-up experience
frustrations: Feeling pressed for time and unable to attend to little chores like grocery shopping, laundry, or cleaning their apartments
Feeling unable to find the specialty food items they like in convenient places
Lack of diversity of food options around their office
data.description: Millennial customers in Latin American megacities are moving into positions of leadership within the economy and are increasingly pressed for time due to the demands of their professional, personal, and social lives.

exhibits.title: Prototyping Examples
exhibits.shows: Four images of low-fidelity prototyping methods used in design practice, including cardboard product prototypes, paper interaction testing for apps, a cardboard fake store setup with facilitators, and a service design prototype for a bakery/restaurant concept.

examples: Cardboard prototype for a Dyson vacuum cleaner
Cardboard boxes designed to create a fake store with facilitators acting as employees to simulate and test a new service design
2nd iteration IDEO service design prototype for a new bakery/restaurant concept

framework: Research: Develop a customer engagement strategy to capture the voice of the customer — including ethnographic interviewing, focus group execution, ethnographic observation, and stakeholder interviews

Synthesis & Design Products: Distill research inputs into insights and design artifacts such as CX journey maps, service design blueprints, and customer personas; establish a collaborative synthesis process

Co-Creation: Design and facilitate workshops for clients/users involving empathy-building exercises, creative presentation of research findings, rapid synthesis for reactions, and small-group solutioning/brainstorming

Prototyping & Scaling: Develop a scrappy, low-budget strategy to test solutions discovered through research and co-creation — options include service design simulation, wireframe testing, A/B testing, and pilot market testing

questions.prompt: Tell me more about your research plan. How do you plan to source users/customers? What kind of questions will you ask them?
questions.guidance: Candidate should articulate a clear plan for recruiting research participants (e.g., intercept recruiting near metro stations, social media outreach, partnering with employers). Questions should probe unmet needs around food access, time constraints, dietary preferences, and current shopping/dining habits. Strong answers address both how to find participants and what types of questions surface latent needs vs. stated preferences.

questions.prompt: Your research team conducted extensive field research in Santiago and Mexico City and distilled insights to identify millennial young professionals as an underserved market in the food space. Given this — what ideas do you have for serving this market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm solutions directly addressing the Exhibit 1 persona's needs and frustrations. Ideas might include: express organic markets near metro stations, meal-kit pick-up lockers at commuter hubs, app-based pre-order and pick-up services, curated specialty food subscription boxes, on-demand delivery to office buildings, bundled ingredient kits optimized for quick weeknight meals. Interviewer should push candidate to generate additional solutions 1-3 times after they stop.

questions.prompt: Given idea [XYZ provided by candidate], how would you test such an idea in a scrappy, cost-effective way? How would you ensure the product or service meets the needs of your target customers?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize this as a prototyping strategy question. Strong answers identify the four required elements: (1) sample users, (2) interactive prototype with test-friendly features, (3) a facilitator, (4) observers. Example answer: build a simulated cardboard storefront with food products the target customer would enjoy, position 2 facilitators to provide service while 2-3 observers record interactions from afar, collect feedback on service/food selection/positioning, test during off-peak hours with volunteers. Excellent candidates note that usability testing outputs feed back into improvement and that the decision point following a test can be framed as Adapt, Adopt, or Abandon.

questions.prompt: Given your idea and the target customer, please size the market for the opportunity in Reforma's major urban markets. Once you size the opportunity, what do you think about these numbers?
questions.guidance: Candidate should either ask for data or state assumptions and work collaboratively with the interviewer to confirm them. The sizing uses: city total population x millennial population % x anticipated penetration rate to get the addressable customer count, then multiply by monthly spend per customer to get monthly revenue. Strong candidates also comment on the sensitivity of the penetration rate assumption and compare market attractiveness across the three cities.

math.setup: For each city: Addressable Customers = Total Population x Millennial % x Penetration Rate; Monthly Revenue = Addressable Customers x Monthly Spend
steps: Bogota: 7,500,000 x 30% x 50% = 1,125,000 (round to 1.1M); Monthly Revenue = 1.1M x $50 = $55M
Mexico City: 8,500,000 x 27% x 20% = 459,000 (round to 0.5M); Monthly Revenue = 0.5M x $300 = $150M
Santiago: 5,500,000 x 30% x 65% = 1,072,500 (round to 1M); Monthly Revenue = 1M x $220 = $220M
math.answer: Monthly revenue opportunity: Bogota $55M, Mexico City $150M, Santiago $220M. Santiago represents the largest monthly revenue opportunity despite having the smallest total population.

brainstorming.prompt: What ideas do you have for serving the millennial urban professional segment identified in the research? What solutions address their needs and frustrations?

categories.name: Convenient pick-up / access points
ideas: Small express organic markets positioned in/around metro stations
Meal-kit pick-up lockers at commuter transit hubs
Pick-up windows or kiosks at office building lobbies
Bundled ingredient grab-and-go stations near co-working spaces

categories.name: Digital / app-based solutions
ideas: App-based pre-order and pick-up for groceries or prepared foods
Subscription service for curated specialty items delivered weekly
On-demand delivery to offices during lunch windows
Digital platform aggregating specialty food vendors near the user

categories.name: Service design / experience
ideas: Express checkout lanes or scan-and-go for time-pressed shoppers
Curated weekly bundles of specialty items aligned to dietary preferences
Personal shopper or concierge grocery service

categories.name: Physical format innovation
ideas: Pop-up markets near offices during morning commute hours
Micro-fulfillment locations embedded in existing retail footprints
Vending-style refrigerated units stocked with premium fresh foods
Partnership with building managers for in-building mini-market installations

recommendation: Reforma should continue prototyping and testing their new B2C food product or service concept, and should prioritize the Santiago market given it represents the largest monthly revenue opportunity ($220M) among the three cities
The team should pursue scrappy low-fidelity prototypes with the millennial urban professional segment before committing capital to full-scale rollout
risks: Penetration rate is purely an estimate and the market size calculations are particularly sensitive to this percentage
Santiago's total population is the smallest compared to Mexico City and Bogota, meaning a shift in the penetration rate assumption has an outsized effect on the revenue estimate
Distribution costs could be higher in Santiago given its positioning in the Andes Mountains
Reforma has no prior B2C experience, which introduces execution and brand-building risk
next_steps: Prototype the service concept in all three cities to identify nuanced differences between consumers
Investigate how consumer needs vary across Mexico City, Santiago, and Bogota
Deploy research teams to all three cities to conduct further field research and prototyping
Define Adapt/Adopt/Abandon criteria before each prototype test to create a structured decision process
